title: Communication
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton's talk emphasizes the importance of letting go of preconceptions and expectations when interacting with others in relationships, particularly in a community setting like the monastery. This "not knowing" allows us to approach others without judgment or attachment, creating space for authentic connection and intimacy. By embracing generosity, radical respect, and self-awareness, we can overcome our negative judgments and cultivate deeper connections with those around us, ultimately promoting well-being for all involved.

sentences.text: This is lemon and honey juice because my voice is so ragged.
I thought maybe I'd try to save it, for your sakes.
And I spilled on my okay, so nothing new.
Dear, dear, good evening.
Yeah, just lemon and honey.
I'm used to it.
I'm really happy to be here this evening and to talk with you a little bit about some experience and learnings that I got at Tassajara Monastery.
For those of you who are new here, Tassajara is a Zen training center monastery in California, and they have two three-month practice periods every year.
This past fall, Chris and another woman, Elizabeth, who is not here this evening, and I went down for this practice period, and it was a big, big experience for each of us.
So I wanted to talk to you a little bit about some of the things that I learned there, particularly about community.
The theme of the fall practice period was living in community, or living in sangha.
Most of the dharma talks had to do with that topic in one way or another.

As some of you know, for the year or so prior to last fall, we here were working on developing policy and procedures for good communications and for conflict resolution, and I was very much involved in that process.
So this was a perfect topic for me down there at Tassajara.
Tassajara is an ongoing community.
Two-thirds of the people who were there during this practice period lived there from one year to four or five or even more years.
They were in their late 20s, lots of them in their 30s, a few in their 40s, and a sprinkling, one or two or three, in their 50s.
So I was really out of range in that situation.
There were lots of relationships that had already been formed: good friends and acquaintances and rivals and loners and enemies, the whole mix of any community.
So when we Tangaryo students arrived, there were 19 of us at first, we had the task of integrating into the community.
The Tangaryo label was for any student who was doing the practice period at Tassajara for the first time.
Some of those people actually lived there, but they had never done the Tangaryo practice period before.
There were 19 of us, and we arrived and had to sit for five days and do nothing else but sit in the zendo, except for sleeping in our beds at night.
Integrating into this community that was already formed was both easier and more difficult because we were in silence much of the time of the practice period.
Our primary focus was to follow the schedule, which was rigorous and tight.
So there wasn't really a lot of time for getting to know each other or socializing.
I'm going to take another scoop of this.
The practice period leaders gave talks mostly about community and relationships and how to think about them.
Christina Lenhair, who was the head of the San Francisco Center, was the head of the practice period.
She's a psychotherapist and a physical therapist.
She is quiet, very intelligent, refined, very kind, but she can also be very direct.

For example, fairly early in the practice period, she made the observation that the coffee and tea area, which was in a kind of center meeting place between the kitchen building and the dining hall, where people could sit around on tables and talk and so forth when we were allowed to talk, was a mess, and she didn't like that.
She said, you live with other people, be kind to them, clean up after yourself.
Don't just rush in there and make a mess and leave.
So she scolded everybody about that.
People began to clean up and it worked really well.
Later on, during one of the sessions, she said, do you realize how loud you are coming up and going out of the zendo?
Be more mindful and be quiet as you step up the steps and go down the steps.
So people began to be a little quieter.
She was kind of the outside observer about community behavior, admonishing us to be kinder to each other.

As I noted above, most of the practice period dharma talks were about living in community, but it turned out that their focus was not on our outward behavior toward each other, but on studying our minds and learning to discipline our minds so that we could support and encourage each other.
That was the topic of my talk tonight.
I'll draw on some of the notes I took at Tassajara, and I'll start with the koan that the teachers used a few times throughout the practice period.
Dizhang's nearness.
*Dizhang asked Fayan, where are you going, senior monk?
Fayan said, I am on pilgrimage.
Dizhang said, what are you on pilgrimage for?
Fayan said, don't know.
Dizhang said, not knowing is most intimate.
Fayan suddenly attained great enlightenment.*
Not knowing is most intimate means that in order to be with what is actually happening, we must not impose our preconceptions on our ever-changing experience.
Same with our relationships with others.
When we don't overlay our fixed ideas on another person, we can see them as they really are and allow them to change as well through time.
Not who we'd like them to be or who we're afraid they are.
When we don't add our expectations and preferences to our interactions with others, we can actually be intimate with them.
So not knowing means getting out of the way so that people can be themselves, and out of our own way so that we can be ourselves moment by moment.
In our sangha life and in our social life in general, not knowing means dropping our ideas about what others are going to do.
For our ideas interpret and distort the truth or reality.
Without our interference, things and people can be what and who they are, and so can we.
The topic of one of the practice period talks by the Tassajara director, Linda Gallahan, was practicing in sangha.
She offered this koan, not knowing is most intimate, as advice to avoid prejudging and holding onto negative opinions about other sangha members.

Our human minds, she said, like to grab onto concepts and judgments about what we experience and to determine what people and things are, and hold these views or stories we have decided are the truth.
Why do we create stories about each other?
The mind does this a lot, she noted.
We make up stories about others and about ourselves for our entertainment.
It's fun to figure out what other people are doing and why.
But more importantly, we do this to feel more in control.
Our minds discriminate among the phenomena that we encounter.
Our minds look for differences to discern what is safe and what is not.
This mental activity originated for our survival, and it still operates that way when necessary.
But the discriminating mind doesn't know when to quit.
It can be a dangerous habit when it is overly active in our relationships,
because the fixed views our minds develop are not current with reality.
They do not reflect what is actually going on with other people and ourselves in the present moment.
This is so because we and all phenomena are always changing.
So our fixed views are never up to date and never accurate.
We really don't know very much about why another person acts the way he or she does, nor sometimes even why we ourselves act as we do.
We don't understand all the causes and conditions of other people's behavior, so we can't really reliably make predictions or evaluations of them.
Nonetheless, our habit of interpreting other people's behavior shapes our behavior toward them.
Because of the way we think about them, we subtly influence them to behave in ways that fulfill our preconception of them.
For instance, my idea is that you won't like me, so when I meet you, because I'm afraid you will reject me, I withhold myself.
I'm not cordial or friendly, and you get the impression that I don't like you.
How's that?
Our expectations can also have a positive outcome.
For instance, when our preconception is that a new person is someone we will like and admire, or do already.
When we have heard good things about someone, or he or she is in a position of power or influence, we might be predisposed to praise or want to please that person.
Thus, our behavior toward them will probably be cordial, which is not a bad thing.
You may have heard of the research on school teachers who are told that their class is an exceptional group of high performers.
Even though they're actually in the bell curve range of good, bad, and indifferent, when the teacher expects them to be really high performers, they turn out to be high performers.
So our impressions about each other really do affect each other in our behavior.
Our preconceptions about other people can be limiting, though, when our expectation is that they will do something wrong or they will disappoint us.
When we interact with people based on our preformed negative judgments about them, we actually limit their behavior by our attitude toward them.
This limiting can be as obvious as when we apply negative archetypes and prejudices to groups or individuals, all the blatant ways in which we blame and separate from others who are not of our tribe.
More commonly, the habit of prejudging and holding fixed views of each other operates very subtly in our daily lives and in our sangha life.

When we judge someone as too young or too old or too intellectual or too easygoing or too technical or too artistic or too whatever for our tastes or needs, we limit how we behave toward them, and thus also limit their options for how they interact and behave toward us.

Or if we develop a negative view of someone because of a difficult interaction that we've had with them in the past, and we let our negative view persist in all our future interactions with them by avoiding them, by not being open with them, by even trying to trick them in some way, we limit them and ourselves.

Our protective and diversionary tactics are usually very subtle and very quick, arising as they do out of our unconscious preconceptions and into expression before we even realize what we are projecting onto the other person.

The Tassajara practice period, three months of living with 46 other people new to me and following a strict and challenging schedule, was a great laboratory for studying the stories my mind makes up when I try to understand other people's behavior, especially when they appear to be behaving negatively toward me.

Because I didn't know anyone at Tassajara besides Chris and Elizabeth, and believe me it was a great support that we were there together, and because following the practice period schedule required my full attention day after day, I never really had enough exposure or information about a given student or teacher to understand the motives for their behavior.
So I learned quite early in the practice period to just drop my stories about them, just let go of it as not useful to me.
In doing this I discovered wonderful new freedoms.
One, I released myself from feeling responsible for their behavior.
That is, I stopped worrying that I must have done something to cause their behavior, et cetera, et cetera.
I released myself from trying to make them like me and also from trying to figure out how to please everyone.
There was just not enough time for any of this, and I even released myself from needing to get to know everyone who was there, though eventually I did get to know everyone to some level.

So giving up my stories, my conceptions and preconceptions about other students and teachers at Tassajara, was very freeing for me, and probably for others because I didn't have any expectations to lay on them.
Now that I'm back home with my established relationships and friendships, I am more attentive to others and what I can do to maintain and further develop my relationships.
However, now when I do have a concern about another person's behavior, I can pretty quickly stop my mind from analyzing and making up my own story.
I can just drop cognizing and wait to see what happens in the next present moment.
It's really freeing.
So how can we open to being present with other people as they are in time, rather than hold preset views of them and limit both us and them?
Linda Galhan urged us to practice, of all things, generosity, to give people the benefit of the doubt.
When we let go of our ideas about other people's motives, we help the other person to change or to simply be who he or she is.
How can we arrive at this don't-know mind and thus intimacy with others?
We can study our own mind.
We can observe our interactions with others.
We can catch ourselves tensing up or preparing for an encounter with someone we don't feel comfortable with and observe what thoughts come up for us.
We can realize we're avoiding eye contact in order not to have to greet and talk with someone.
There are a myriad of ways in which we can manifest our judgments about people and allow our behavior to limit their options as well as our own.
So sangha practice offers us a safe place to study our minds and to change how they operate.

We can observe our mind and catch it in the act of resisting or turning away, and instead drop our prejudgment and be neutral at least, or more proactively, we can practice generosity and give people we've been wary of the benefit of the doubt instead of continuing to be stuck in our fixed view of them.
Let our negative judgments go.
Just be in the present and experience whatever happens.
Of course at first, and maybe for a long time, we won't notice our negative concepts about others until after we have reacted to them in a way we later regret.
When we find ourselves wishing that we hadn't been sarcastic, or hadn't diminished another's concern, or hadn't joked about something it turned out the other person was serious about, we feel bad.
But this is the first step toward changing our mental life and after that our behavior.
When we realize we have made a mistake, we can then examine ourselves to discover what concepts and prejudices led to it, and we can vow to catch ourselves next time and not make that mistake again.
Sometimes it takes making this mistake many, many times, but eventually with mindfulness we will be able to overcome this bad habit and change both our thinking and our behavior.
And of course somewhere in there we can also apologize to the person we've offended.
Sangha life is being with others who are trying to live authentically and compassionately.
So we know we can give each other the benefit of the doubt.
Sangha life is the perfect place to practice the not knowing that leads to intimacy.
The abbess Christina Lerher gave several very helpful dharma talks about how our minds work.
Her first talk on this shed light on how our thinking prevents us from being intimate with others, from experiencing each other and ourselves as we actually are.
She said we don't actually know what will happen with another person even though we think we do know.
As in, oh, he snubbed me yesterday, so today I'm not going to look at him so he doesn't hurt my feelings again.
Christina said our fixed views of people create repetitive experiences.
They keep us stuck in old paradigms.
Actual experience, she said, can only be experienced, not conceived.
When we tell about an event, it is not the same as experiencing it.
An idea is not reality.
Knowing is outside of experience and an add-on to experience.
Thus the point that not knowing is intimate.
When we do something based on an idea, we limit ourselves to our preconceptions.
Before we act, we should check out what actually is reality.
Christina quoted the poet David Waggoner, who wrote, quote,
*treat everything and everyone as a powerful stranger to be respected.*
*Treat everyone and everything as a powerful stranger to be respected.*
For intimacy to happen, radical respect is required.
Be open to what presents itself rather than knowing and thus restricting what will happen.
In another talk, Christina told us that individual practice actually depends on sangha practice.
We really can't practice alone.
As sangha members, she admonished us to support each other in our practice.
We should see each other as teachers pointing to our mind's habitual perceptions and preferences.
We should practice radical acceptance and respect for each other in order to encourage each other's individual practice.
Having respect, she said, means not interpreting other people's behavior.
Leave it alone, and again, interpreting limits both us and the ones we interpret.
In this connection she offered a couple of examples that she probably drew from her observations of us in the practice period.
She said, one, fantasizing, and fantasizing was a pretty big habit at the monastery, fantasizing about someone else is actually treating him or her as an object for your entertainment.
It's meddling in the other person's boundaries.
It puts pressure on him or her.
It distracts him or her from practice.
Don't do that.
Acting as a self-appointed teacher or boss of others also imposes a burden on them and violates their boundaries.
Don't do that.

Asking someone to keep a secret about someone else imposes a burden on the person you're asking to keep the secret, to think about that person differently than they would if they didn't know the secret.
Don't do that.

Instead, Christina advised, when we realize we're making up a story about someone, which may lead us to use or invade that person, we should instead become interested in why we need to make up the story.
After all, it's our story.
Once we understand what we're doing, then we can let go of the story without having exploited anyone else in the process.
Christina acknowledged that such self-examination takes courage, both to look at ourselves and to accept our bad habits.
But this is exactly how we can support each other.
This is the opportunity that living in sangha gives us.
She pointed out that our meal chant, which we chanted at Tassajara three times a day, begins with the words,
*in trusting ourselves to the Sangha.*
In trusting ourselves means depending on the Sangha for our well-being.
Our actions that support the Sangha safeguard everyone and promote well-being for everyone, ourselves included.
I hope these little bits of Tassajara teachings can be helpful to us as we continue to practice together in Sangha, in trusting ourselves to each other.
Thank you.
*Deeply extend to everybody.
With the true...
Beings are possible...*

Instead, Christina advised, when we realize we're making up a story about someone, which may lead us to use or invade that person,

we should instead become interested in why we need to make up the story. After all, it's our story. Once we understand what we're doing, then we can let go of the story without having exploited anyone else in the process. Christina acknowledged that such self-examination takes courage both to look at ourselves and to accept our bad habits. But this is exactly how we can support each other. This is the opportunity that living in Sangha gives us. She pointed out that our meal chant, which we chanted at Tassajara three times a day, begins with the words, in trusting ourselves to the Sangha.

In trusting ourselves means depending on the Sangha for our well-being. Our actions that support the Sangha safeguard everyone and promote well-being for everyone, ourselves included. I hope these little bits of Tassajara teachings can be helpful to us as we continue to practice together in Sangha, in trusting ourselves to each other. Thank you. Deeply extend to everybody.
